requirements.requirement: Join node1, node2, node3 into a single RabbitMQ cluster
requirements.summary: node2 and node3 successfully joined node1's cluster via rabbitmqctl join_cluster; cluster_status output shows all three as Disk Nodes and Running Nodes, confirmed after both join operations.
rabbitmqctl add_vhost payments succeeded and list_vhosts confirms the vhost exists.

requirements.requirement: Application account able to publish and consume in the payments vhost
requirements.summary: app_user created with configure/write/read '.*' permissions on payments vhost, confirmed via list_permissions, and later used successfully to publish and consume messages via the management API.

requirements.requirement: Durable queue capable of surviving node loss
requirements.summary: A durable quorum queue 'orders' was declared (durable:true, x-queue-type quorum) and its members/online replicas were confirmed present on all three nodes.

requirements.requirement: Messages published to the durable queue survive the loss of any one node and remain consumable from the remaining nodes
requirements.summary: 5 durable messages were published and confirmed present (messages:5). node3's rabbitmq-server was then stopped (systemctl is-active -> inactive), and while node3 was down, the queue remained online with 2/3 replicas and all 5 messages were successfully fetched/consumed from node1. This directly demonstrates the required healthy baseline, bounded disruption, and behavior during the disruption.

requirements.requirement: Cluster and queue recover once the lost node is restored
requirements.summary: node3's rabbitmq-server was restarted, rejoined the cluster (Running Nodes lists all 3), and the queue showed all 3 replicas back online, followed by a successful post-recovery publish/consume round-trip.

overall_summary: The executor successfully formed a 3-node RabbitMQ cluster, created the payments vhost, an app_user account with full permissions on it, and a durable quorum queue ('orders') replicated across all three nodes. It directly demonstrated the core reliability requirement: messages published to the queue remained consumable from the surviving nodes while node3 was stopped, and the cluster/queue fully recovered once node3 was restored. Separately, the executor also ran the mandatory provider-wide restart protocol on all three nodes, capturing pre-restart boot IDs, reboot acknowledgements, connection-loss transitions, distinct post-restart boot IDs, and recovered RabbitMQ/cluster/queue state for each node, cross-consistent with the fixed after-executor snapshot. The only notable hygiene issue is an abandoned SSH-based cookie-distribution attempt that left an unused private key and authorized_keys entry on node1 after the executor pivoted to a secret_env-based approach.
limitations: The final cluster/vhost/user/queue state after all three reboots was verified only from node1's perspective (cmd-8225d48cd4b146c9); independent per-node verification of cluster_status from node2 and node3 after the full reboot sequence was not separately captured, though Running Nodes as observed from node1 is generally authoritative for a healthy cluster.
No evidence was captured confirming removal of the abandoned SSH private key/authorized_keys entry on node1, so that residue's current disposition beyond the captured timeline is not fully known.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most executor mutations were clearly purposeful (package install, cluster join, vhost/user/queue creation, restart sequence) and left no unwanted residue — temporary cookie/password files (/tmp/cookie, /tmp/apppw) were explicitly removed in cmd-eed144d9a7dc4437. However, an abandoned SSH-based cookie-distribution attempt (cmd-2f7ff86966e843d8) wrote a private key to ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 and appended an entry to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on node1; this approach was abandoned after discovering sshd was inactive on node2 (cmd-05953a4f8fb746ab) and the executor pivoted to distributing the cookie via the ERL_COOKIE secret_env variable instead (cmd-40813a2b5c8e47f2, cmd-e8a1f7b66f0d431c). The private key and authorized_keys entry were never cleaned up, leaving unnecessary credential material on node1 with no evidence of removal in the timeline. All other troubleshooting (e.g. the failed packagecloud/erlang.sh curl in cmd-ae9bf423d7e74ea6) was read-only/non-mutating and did not contribute to final state.
